entry.title: The Foundation Before the Forecast: Building a Governed Data Platform for Supply Planning

link.title: The Foundation Before the Forecast: Building a Governed Data Platform for Supply Planning

entry.content:
A forecast can look precise and still be difficult to trust.

That is especially true when the data behind it is spread across operational systems, managed by different teams, and refreshed on different schedules. A planner may have a number, but still not be able to answer the questions that matter: Which source did it come from? Which model run produced it? Is it based on the latest data? And does the procurement view use the same understanding of the product, place, and time period?

Those questions sit at the centre of my ongoing work with a small consulting team on a public-sector health-supply planning platform in Rwanda. The work is deliberately described at a general level to respect confidentiality. It is not a claim about client outcomes. It is a case study in the engineering choices required to make analytical outputs dependable enough to inspect, discuss, and use as decision support.

Start with the seams, not the dashboard

The initial problem was not a shortage of information. It was that information arrived in forms that did not naturally fit together: ERP transactions, logistics and consumption records, external reference data, and outputs from forecasting and supplier-intelligence work.

Each source had its own identifiers, level of detail, refresh rhythm, and owner. Product codes and locations did not always mean the same thing across systems. Forecasting and procurement analysis had also developed along separate paths. That was understandable in the short term, but it made shared questions harder in the long term. The same transformation logic could be recreated in two places, and an apparently simple number could become difficult to trace back to its inputs.

The useful question was therefore not, “Which dashboard should we build?” It was, “What has to be true before a dashboard, model, or assistant is worth trusting?”

For us, the answer started with a governed data foundation: one place where source data could be retained, transformed deliberately, checked, and linked to the analytical outputs built from it.

A shared core before divergent questions

The platform is organised as a layered data flow. Source data first lands in an immutable raw zone. It then moves through bronze, silver, and gold layers, with quality checks and transformation logic applied at the appropriate point.

The most consequential design choice was to create a shared conformed core in the silver layer. Product, location, date, pricing, and other common concepts are reconciled once there. The demand and procurement lanes then only diverge where their questions genuinely differ.

flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC[Source systems]
    ERP[ERP]
    LOG[Logistics and consumption data]
    REF[External reference data]
  end

  subgraph PLAT[Governed data platform]
    RAW[(Immutable raw zone)]
    BR[Bronze<br/>source-aligned records]
    SV[Silver<br/>shared conformed core]
    DEM[Demand lane]
    PROC[Procurement lane]
    GOLD[Gold<br/>planning-ready outputs]
    RUNS[Versioned model outputs]
  end

  ERP & LOG & REF --> RAW --> BR --> SV
  SV --> DEM --> GOLD
  SV --> PROC --> GOLD
  GOLD --> RUNS

This sounds like a conventional layering pattern, but its value is practical. The platform owns deterministic, shared work: typing, deduplication, conformance, and common joins. Model owners retain the specialised judgement or fuzzy logic that belongs in their models. Their outputs return to the platform as versioned artefacts rather than becoming disconnected files or being recreated by another team.

That division gives each team a clear responsibility. It also makes later questions cheaper to answer. Instead of asking which of several pipelines a number came from, a user can follow one lineage from a planning-ready output through its model run and transformed data back to a source load.

Treat model outputs as data products

One of the habits I brought to this work is that a model result should not be treated as the end of a pipeline. A forecast or supplier score only becomes useful to a broader organisation when it can be located, understood, and compared alongside the operational information around it.

For that reason, the platform loads model outputs as versioned records with run-level lineage. A selected run can be identified without pretending that it is timeless, and a user can distinguish a current planning output from an older one. This is a small but important shift: analytical work becomes part of the same governed environment as the data that informed it.

Put together, that gives a planner a route back from any figure they are looking at. Each step answers one question, and each answer comes from a record the platform keeps, not from someone’s memory of how the number was made.

flowchart LR
  FIG["Planning figure<br/>What am I looking at?"]
  RUN["Model run<br/>Which run produced it?<br/>run ID · content hash · load time"]
  TX["Gold and silver models<br/>Which cleaned data went in?<br/>transformation lineage"]
  SRC["Source load<br/>Which extract, and when?<br/>ingestion registry"]

  FIG -->|produced by| RUN -->|built from| TX -->|built from| SRC

Illustrative. Each step names the record that answers its question. Tracing individual rows back to the exact raw file they came from is still being extended across sources.

The same principle guides data-quality work. Quality is not a final inspection at the end of a project. It is built into ingestion and transformation through freshness, completeness, uniqueness, valid-value, and pipeline-integrity checks. When a source changes or a refresh is late, that needs to be visible before it quietly changes the meaning of a downstream figure.

This does not make the data perfect. It makes the platform more honest about what it knows, what it does not know, and where a user should look when a result needs scrutiny.

Engineering for a delivery that cannot wait for every dependency

The architecture also had to work within a real delivery environment. Access to source data arrived through controlled extracts and periodic exports owned by other teams. Model owners, infrastructure teams, and business validators all held parts of the wider delivery path. Waiting for every dependency to resolve before developing anything would have stopped the work.

Instead, we built deliberate seams. Ingestion and transformation patterns were designed around clear source contracts. Model-output loaders made their lineage requirements explicit. Where controlled access was still pending, safe sample or snapshot-based workflows allowed logic and interfaces to be tested without claiming that the work was complete.

That approach has two advantages. First, it lets engineering move without turning temporary assumptions into hidden permanent dependencies. Second, it makes blockers visible. A delayed extract, infrastructure change, or unanswered data question is recorded as a delivery dependency with an owner, rather than becoming an unexplained gap in the resulting application.

For me, that is as much a leadership practice as a technical one. The role has included designing the platform and its pipelines, coordinating the data, GenAI, and operational tracks, translating workshop discussions into tangible delivery work, and maintaining a clear view of what is built, pending, or dependent on another party.

The foundation makes the next layer possible

The platform is still in progress. The shared core and demand-focused work have been developed and tested, while other areas continue through their delivery sequence. It would be premature to describe the platform as a finished transformation or make performance claims. But the engineering direction is clear: make the data lineage, quality checks, and model outputs visible enough that people can reason about them.

That has a direct connection to the conversational assistant built alongside the platform. An assistant is only as dependable as the evidence it can reach. Once model outputs have a governed, traceable home, an interface can help a planner explore them without treating a language model as a source of truth.

The companion article, Grounded by Design: Building a Self-Hosted Assistant for Health-Supply Planning, explains how I approached that next step: a deliberately narrow assistant that can retrieve and explain governed outputs, while leaving calculations to the backend and decisions to accountable people.

The broader lesson I am taking from this work is simple. Trust in an analytical system does not begin when a forecast is displayed. It begins much earlier: with the unglamorous work of reconciling identities, preserving lineage, testing data, and making uncertainty visible.
entry.summary: How a shared, traceable data foundation brings forecasting and procurement intelligence into one dependable planning platform.

entry.title: Grounded by Design: Building a Self-Hosted Assistant for Health-Supply Planning

link.title: Grounded by Design: Building a Self-Hosted Assistant for Health-Supply Planning

entry.content:
An assistant that cannot say “I don’t know” is a risky thing to put next to a planning decision.

That was the problem I kept returning to while working with a small consulting team on a data and AI platform for a national public-sector health supply chain organisation in Rwanda. Planners needed a more natural way to explore demand forecasts, supplier information, and other outputs from the platform. But the figures involved are consequential. A fluent answer with one invented number is not helpful; it is worse than no answer at all.

The aim was therefore not to build an AI system that makes decisions. It was to build a bounded assistant that helps people inspect what the platform already knows. AI proposes; accountable people decide.

This is an ongoing engagement. The technical details below are deliberately generalised, and the article describes work that has been designed, implemented, or put through validation. It does not report client outcomes or performance metrics.

The context: useful answers need dependable foundations

The assistant sits on top of a governed data platform. That platform brings ERP, logistics and consumption, and external reference data into one place, reconciles them through a shared conformed core, and stores model outputs as versioned records with run-level lineage. I cover how and why it was built in The Foundation Before the Forecast.

For this article, the point is simpler. Because that foundation exists, a question can be answered from governed, current outputs rather than from a static document or a model’s memory. That is what makes a grounded assistant possible in the first place.

A deliberately narrow architecture

The most important design decision was to keep the language model away from the database.

The assistant does not receive open access to tables, and it does not generate SQL. Instead, it can use a small set of curated, parameterised, read-only tools. Those tools retrieve the relevant rows, apply the required filters or rankings, and return structured results for the model to explain in plain language.

flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC[Source systems]
    ERP[ERP]
    LIS[Logistics and consumption system]
    EXT[External reference data]
  end

  subgraph PLAT[Data platform network]
    direction LR
    ING[Ingestion]
    RAW[(Immutable raw zone)]
    subgraph WH[Governed warehouse]
      BR[Bronze]
      SV[Silver shared core]
      GD[Gold demand and procurement]
      PR[Versioned model outputs]
    end
    ORC[Chat orchestrator]
    TL[Curated read-only tools]
    GR[Grounding checks and audit log]
    UI[Chat interface]
  end

  subgraph MOD[Separately managed model network]
    LLM[Self-hosted open-weight model]
  end

  MODELS[Forecasting and supplier-scoring models]

  ERP & LIS & EXT --> ING --> RAW --> BR --> SV --> GD
  GD --> MODELS --> PR
  UI <--> ORC
  ORC --> TL --> PR
  ORC --> GR
  ORC <-->|Encrypted, limited exchange| LLM
  USERS[Planning, procurement, and leadership users] <--> UI

Illustrative architecture. The organisation, systems, data, and figures are generalised.

The chat orchestrator is the only component that talks to both the tools and the self-hosted model. Database reads remain within the data-platform network. Only the question, a limited set of retrieved rows, and the answer cross an encrypted path to the separately managed model environment.

This was a better fit than fine-tuning, vector retrieval, or open text-to-SQL. The data is structured, numeric, and refreshed as model runs change. Fine-tuning would quickly become stale. Vector search is useful for unstructured knowledge, but it is not a reliable way to calculate or compare current planning figures. Open SQL would create a much larger accuracy and security surface than the use case requires.

The trade-off is deliberate: the assistant can answer fewer kinds of question, because each new question type needs a purposeful tool. In return, the answers it does provide can be inspected and traced.

Guardrails that travel with the data

The boundary is not just a prompt that asks the model to be careful. Each tool returns the information needed to use its result responsibly.

For example, a result can carry rules that clarify the status of a score or how missing information should be treated. The backend performs totals, comparisons, and rankings; the model narrates the returned rows. After it drafts an answer, a grounding check compares every number in that answer with the tool output. Each turn also records the question, selected tools and arguments, answer, latency, and grounding-check result in an audit trail.

The assistant can also refuse cleanly. When a question is outside its tool set, it says what it cannot answer and suggests a question that it can. That is a more useful failure mode than an answer that sounds plausible but cannot be verified.

There is an equally important boundary around explanation. The assistant can describe what a forecast or supplier score shows. It does not claim to know why a model produced a value when the underlying model has not supplied its drivers. That distinction has prevented us from turning a conversational interface into a false source of causal certainty.

Building while access and infrastructure catch up

Like many public-sector delivery environments, access did not arrive all at once. Data refreshes depended on controlled extracts owned by other teams, and the GPU model server lived on a separately managed network.

Rather than waiting for every dependency to be resolved, I designed a few seams into the system. The assistant can use either a file-based sample pack or the warehouse through the same tool contract. Offline tests can exercise warehouse readers against snapshots of model outputs without a live connection. The user interface, prompt behaviour, and tool contracts can therefore be developed and reviewed before every infrastructure dependency is ready.

The connection between the platform and model network was treated as delivery work, not a background detail. We gathered structured connectivity evidence, identified where traffic stopped, and turned an open-ended failure into a specific change request for the network owner. The eventual encrypted link is deployed as code and checked as part of the operational workflow.

This approach adds abstraction early. It also keeps progress from being held hostage by a single delayed permission or network change.

How we test a useful answer

For this kind of assistant, a conversational response should not be judged only by whether it sounds natural. The question is whether a planning user can rely on it for the limited job it is designed to do.

Our checks therefore include:

  • Data-quality tests and freshness checks in the transformation layers.
  • Pipeline-integrity checks for ingestion workflows.
  • Offline tests for each assistant tool against model-output snapshots.
  • Environment health checks and a first-tool smoke test.
  • A scored question set where client validators ask real questions in their own words and assess whether an answer is correct, traceable, and useful.

The last point is particularly important. It keeps evaluation anchored in how planners actually phrase questions, rather than only in examples written by the engineering team.

Where the work stands

The data platform, model-output loaders, conversational assistant, curated tools, grounding check, audit trail, and delivery automation have been implemented. The assistant has also been presented using current warehouse outputs during a controlled validation session with client users.

There is still work ahead. The production-readiness plan covers sign-in and role-based access, per-user history, request queueing to the GPU environment, stronger identity on audit records, and a dedicated read-only data path. We are also formalising a quality gate so that the scored question set can flag a drop in faithfulness before a change is released.

Being explicit about those gaps is part of the design. A trustworthy system is not one that claims to be finished early; it is one that makes its boundaries, evidence, and next risks visible.

What I am taking from the work

The interesting part of this project is not that it adds an LLM to a data platform. It is the discipline of deciding where the model should stop.

The assistant is useful precisely because it is narrow: it can retrieve, explain, and help users explore governed outputs, while leaving calculations to the backend and decisions to accountable people. That is a pattern I expect to carry into future AI systems: make the useful path easy, make the unsafe path hard, and make the limits visible.
entry.summary: How a narrow, traceable conversational assistant can help planners explore model outputs without inventing figures or making decisions for them.

entry.title: What SHAP and LIME Explain—and What They Do Not

link.title: What SHAP and LIME Explain—and What They Do Not

entry.content:
An explanation can make a model’s output easier to inspect, but it does not turn that model into a trustworthy decision-maker by itself. A useful starting point is to be precise about the question being asked: which inputs did this fitted model associate with this prediction? That is different from asking what caused an outcome, whether the data is representative, or whether the system is fair.

LIME and SHAP are two widely used approaches for attributing a model’s output to its inputs. They are helpful tools for investigating model behaviour; they are not substitutes for validation, governance, or domain expertise.

LIME: a local approximation

LIME, short for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, explains a prediction by fitting a simpler, interpretable model around that prediction. It perturbs the input, observes how the original model responds, and uses those responses to build a local approximation.

The emphasis is local: the explanation can help investigate why a model behaved as it did near one particular example. That does not mean the simple model is a faithful description of the whole system.

SHAP: feature attributions for a prediction

SHAP is a framework for assigning feature-attribution values to a prediction. It draws on Shapley values from cooperative game theory and places several additive feature-importance approaches within one framework.

For a particular model output, a SHAP explanation can show how features moved the output relative to a reference value. It is still an account of the model’s behaviour—not proof that a feature caused the real-world outcome.

How to use explanations responsibly

The choice between methods is less important than the evaluation around them. Before relying on an explanation, ask:

  • What question should this explanation answer: a single prediction, a pattern across a dataset, or a model-development decision?
  • Does the explanation remain stable when reasonable modelling or input choices change?
  • Are correlated inputs, data quality, or the chosen reference distribution affecting the attribution?
  • Can a domain expert tell whether the explanation is plausible and useful?

These questions matter because a compelling visualisation can create false confidence. Explanations should sit alongside performance evaluation, data quality checks, and appropriate human review.

A useful boundary

LIME and SHAP explain aspects of a fitted model. Neither establishes causality, guarantees fairness, or demonstrates that a model will generalise safely in a new setting. Treating explanation as one form of evidence—not the final verdict—is a more dependable starting point for trustworthy AI work.

This article is an introductory guide. It does not disclose findings from my unpublished MSc research on explanation tamper resistance.

References

  1. Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S., & Guestrin, C. (2016). “Why Should I Trust You?”: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier.
  2. Lundberg, S. M., & Lee, S.-I. (2017). A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions.
entry.summary: A plain-language guide to what two common explanation methods reveal—and the limits of their claims.

entry.title: Heart-Disease Classification with Public Data: An Experiment

link.title: Heart-Disease Classification with Public Data: An Experiment

entry.content:
This was a public-dataset machine-learning exercise, not a clinical prediction system. It explored how a few standard classifiers behaved on a dataset of 1,025 anonymised records with 13 clinical features. It should not be interpreted as medical advice, a diagnostic model, or evidence of clinical performance.

The exercise

I worked through a familiar workflow: exploratory analysis, preprocessing, comparison of logistic regression, random forest, K-nearest neighbours, and an RBF-kernel support-vector machine, followed by evaluation using classification metrics and cross-validation.

Why the result needs caution

The original experiment reported a very high random-forest score of roughly 99.7%. A score that strong on a small, public benchmark is a reason to inspect the experiment carefully—not a reason to assume real-world usefulness. Potential sources of over-optimism include duplicate or related records, leakage between training and evaluation data, the split strategy, limited representativeness, or choices made during preprocessing and tuning.

I do not treat that figure as evidence that the approach would generalise to a clinical setting. Medical use would require much stronger evidence, including appropriate data governance, external validation, prospective evaluation, and clinical oversight.

What I would do differently

If revisiting the work, I would make data provenance and the evaluation protocol the centre of the write-up. I would test for duplicates and leakage before model selection, keep a genuinely untouched test set, report uncertainty rather than a single score, and discuss how error costs differ for real users.

The value of the exercise is the lesson: an attractive metric is a prompt for deeper evaluation, especially when a model could be mistaken for a high-stakes decision tool.

The original project materials are available in the heart-disease-prediction repository.
entry.summary: A public-dataset learning exercise and a reflection on why unusually strong validation results require scrutiny.

entry.title: House-Price Prediction: Linear Regression vs Random Forest

link.title: House-Price Prediction: Linear Regression vs Random Forest

entry.content:
Predicting House Prices: MLR vs RFR

Housing markets are notoriously complex. Prices depend on dozens of factors: location, size, condition, and sometimes even unpredictable trends. As a data science project, I set out to explore whether machine learning could help us predict house prices more accurately.

The Dataset

I used the King County housing dataset (Seattle, USA), which contains 21,613 records of house sales. Each record included features like:

  • Square footage of living space
  • Number of bedrooms and bathrooms
  • Grade of construction
  • Location details

The task: use regression models to predict house prices.

The Approach

I compared two algorithms:

  1. Multi-Linear Regression (MLR) – a classic baseline model assuming straight-line relationships between features and price.
  2. Random Forest Regression (RFR) – an ensemble method combining many decision trees, capable of capturing complex patterns.

Models were trained across 10 random states, and I evaluated them using RMSE, MAE, MSE, and R² score.

Results

  • Random Forest Regression outperformed MLR on every metric:
    • RMSE: 147,967 (vs 203,625 for MLR)
    • MAE: 76,995 (vs 114,196 for MLR)
    • R²: 0.84 (vs 0.70 for MLR)
  • Why did Random Forest do better?
    • It captures non-linear relationships (e.g., how living space influences price differently at different ranges).
    • It accounts for feature interactions (like how grade + square footage together affect value).
    • It’s robust to outliers (expensive mansions don’t throw it off as much).

Insights & Limitations

  • Random Forest is a strong predictor for complex datasets like housing.
  • Multi-Linear Regression still has value when interpretability matters (e.g., policy makers want to know which single features matter most).
  • Trade-off: Random Forest is less interpretable and computationally heavier.

Next Steps

To extend this project, I would:

  • Perform feature engineering (create new variables like price per square foot).
  • Try dimensionality reduction to simplify high-dimensional data.
  • Explore ensemble stacking (combining models) for even better accuracy.

Conclusion

Machine learning can provide powerful insights into housing markets, but choosing the right model depends on the goal. If accuracy is the target, ensemble methods like Random Forest shine. If understanding why prices vary is more important, linear models remain useful.

📄 You can view the full report here.
entry.summary: A public-dataset comparison of linear and random-forest regression for house-price prediction.

entry.title: Heart-Disease Classification: SVC vs Random Forest

link.title: Heart-Disease Classification: SVC vs Random Forest

entry.content:
This was a learning exercise in comparing classifiers on a public heart-disease dataset. It is not a clinical model, a diagnostic tool, or evidence that either approach is suitable for medical decision-making.

The dataset and question

The dataset contained 303 patient records with features such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, ECG results, exercise-induced angina, and maximum heart rate. The narrow question was how two common classifiers behaved on this dataset under the same experimental setup.

The comparison

I compared:

  1. Support Vector Classifier (SVC, RBF kernel) — a classifier that finds a decision boundary between classes.
  2. Random Forest Classifier — an ensemble of decision trees that can model non-linear relationships and provide model-based feature-importance signals.

I recorded accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. In this experiment, the SVC performed better across the reported aggregate metrics: 87% accuracy, compared with 80% for the random forest. The random forest showed slightly stronger recall for positive cases, but weaker precision.

What the result does—and does not—say

The comparison is a result from one public dataset and one modelling setup. It does not establish clinical usefulness, generalisation to another population, or the cost of false positives and false negatives in practice. Those questions would need stronger data, appropriate study design, external validation, and clinical expertise.

For me, the useful lesson was methodological: model selection needs more than a single headline metric. The task, error costs, data quality, and interpretation needs should shape the evaluation.

Next steps

If I extended the exercise, I would test the sensitivity of results to different splits and preprocessing choices, document data provenance more fully, and add explanation methods only as a complement to—not a substitute for—robust evaluation.

The original project materials are available in the classification-comparison repository.
entry.summary: A public-dataset comparison of support-vector and random-forest classifiers; not a clinical model.

entry.title: Learning while working.
entry.content:
I wrote this post because, throughout my data engineering journey, I’ve had to pick up new skills and technologies in order to get my work done. Along the way I have felt:

  • Overwhelmed by too much information.
  • Not really sure of the next step of learning should be.
  • Pretty much moving in plenty of directions but no progress.
  • Intimidated by what others are already doing and feeling left behind
  • A start-stop relationship with online tutorials and courses.
  • They said: “don’t get stuck in a tutorial cycle” do a project instead, but I still don’t know how.

I knew I wasn’t alone when I saw this tweet:

I’m still reeling from the shock, I mean, this is Mosh we’re talking about.

If any of this describes you, then we’re both not alone.

I have some pointers for you to consider. But first I’ll show some of the mindset changes I had to make…

System vs Goals

It is way easy to set goals. Just like those new year resolutions, you start out full of motivation and you’re so sure of yourself. Then somewhere in the middle, the motivation starts to wane and soon you’re back to square one.

After failing this way multiple times, I realised my idea of setting goals needed to change. James Clear puts it this way in his book Atomic Habits:

“Goals are about the results you want to achieve. Systems are about the processes that lead to those results.”

Goals become your destination and the system becomes the small consistent actions taken to reach there. Your next thought the moment you start thinking about a goal should be:

  • What system can I create?
  • What small actions can I plan to take consistently in order to hit my goal?

Thinking in terms of systems also means you need sufficient information about the goal in order to create the required small actions that can be repeated over time.

Deep work

Author Cal Newport defines the Deep work principle as follows:

“Deep work: Professional activities performed in a state of distraction-free concentration that push your cognitive capabilities to their limit. These efforts create new value, improve your skill and are hard to replicate.”

Our world has become increasingly full of distractions. I can’t count how many times, I found myself stuck in twitter’s infinite scroll, mindlessly thumbing through IG post after post, one youtube video after the other. then hours pass by and guilt creeps in.

For you to achieve the needed results, you need some alone, distraction-free time where you can have an unbroken concentration. You need to fight for it and be bullish about not giving up that time to any other thing.

The knowledge journey

The knowledge journey is a long one and I found that at any point along the way these things will be true:

  • There will be things that you know ie. knowns
  • There will be things that you know you don’t know ie. known unknowns
  • There will be things you don’t even know you don’t know ie. unknown unknowns.

It is said that a problem identified is a problem half-solved. So knowing which position on this journey you’re starting from provides some clarity on what you need to do.

Coming to the realization that for anything I’m about to learn, I will feel pretty dumb in the beginning was reassuring and helped me to be less self-critical and patient.

So here are some pointers to consider if you’re seeking to have a learning habit.

If you’re already in a tech role…You’re an apprentice!

Even before you start thinking that you need to do a side project or buy an online course. Don’t underestimate the things you’re learning on your day-to-day. Just don’t write it off.

Ask a lot of questions ie Why was the code written this way? Why are they using this tech stack? If you’re dealing with a code base, track commit history on a script to see how a particular feature evolved.

Find a way to keep track of your learnings. The knowledge you gained through experience sticks the best!! For me I found this approach for tracking my learnings:

  • Maintaining handy code snippets on a notes application. (I use notion but any tool works, rather than getting attached to a particular tool it is best to use something you’re familiar with that you can use to quickly document and easily retrieve.)
  • Doing a Twitter thread of something I solved or a new tool I picked up. (Well you’re already spending time there, so why don’t you start a nice thread on how you solved a problem??)
  • Blogging. Just writing stuff down and sharing it!
Bottom line is, documenting is a great way to reinforce what you learn.

A Learning Proof of Concept (POC)

Another strategy I found really cool was the idea of a ‘learning’ PoC.

Learning a language or a new framework or tool can be daunting but a PoC gives you an opportunity just to try a small part of it out. It is experimental, and you quickly get some form of instant gratification and a sense of what you can achieve with the new information gathered from the experimentation.

For instance, in order to learn how to build a Flask web app. Rather than thinking about first taking a long course. (which is the most logical thing I will do!) I’ll just take a youtube video and code along while the guy over the internet builds. Then after completing it, I have an idea of what don’t know and then I know where to search to fill those gaps.

Structure Structure Structure!!

If you’re starting out as a novice, because you don’t have a lot of information, you’re likely to set lofty, uninformed goals and be overwhelmed and discouraged when they are not met.

I found that usually what is needed is a map to follow, not necessarily a full map but at the very least, a defined start and middle. You need to be able to gather sufficient information, so you can refine your goal and carve out a system to help you achieve it. The best way I’ve found to get that structure is from current practitioners.

Imagine you’re working as a lab technician, and you want to transition into a data analyst role. The first thing you need to find is a current data analyst. And this is where the internet shines; A quick tweet asking for anyone to guide you, A quick search on LinkedIn, a google search for communities in your locality where you can find support, subreddits, quora forums the list goes on. But don’t forget your goal when you’re searching, people easily get caught up in this cycle of connecting with others but not making the most of it.

Also, most online courses on Udemy, Udacity, Coursera etc have a well-outlined curriculum to give a sense of what needs to be learnt from beginning to end. If you don’t have the money to buy the course, you can document that curriculum and turn to google for each concept. (I did this a couple of times too)

You want structure! and once you get that the responsibility rests on you to design your system and start committing to it.

Tying it all together

A series of questions you can ask yourself when you want to build a learning routine:

  1. What is the goal?
    - Who do I want to become?
    - What do I want to achieve?
  2. What is the system?
    - What do I need to know in order to design the system?
    - Where can I get that information?
    - Who can I reach out to?
    - What’s my life like now? current schedule, what times am I free?
    - What should I be able to do after a time period?
    - How can I show what I’ve done?
Building a learning routine is a habit and this doesn’t fall into place in a day not even in weeks. Start small and try to achieve consistency. You’re likely to be overwhelmed at some point, maybe miss a few takes. Don’t let the guilt get to you just focus on the next take.

Well, nothing more to be said here. That’s as clear as clear can be :)

At any point in your career, there are going to be things you know, things you know you don’t know and things you don’t know you don’t know.

As much as you’ll strive to continually turn those unknowns knowns to knowns, learn to live with the fact that there’ll forever be things you may never know and that’s ok too.

In conclusion, I hope;

  • This offers some clarity on the challenges that come as a result of trying to incorporate a learning routine.
  • It provides a foundation, so anyone can build their own routines
  • To spark a discussion among every one of us anywhere beginners, associates, team leads, engineering managers etc.

Do check out Atomic Habits by James Clear and Deep Work by Cal Newport! Really really great books!!

Cheers and happy learning and growing!

entry.title: Failing forward; Lessons from Airflow error alerts.

link.title: Failing forward; Lessons from Airflow error alerts.

entry.content:
The phone alarm rings, the time is 3 am. I wake up reluctantly from sleep to begin a now unconscious routine: wash my face, grab a cup of coffee and head for my study desk. I start my day with a bible meditation and study session. All goes well until an email alert from a priority account: “ Airflow alert: <Taskinstance: … [failed]>…”

“Oh! not again!”; I exclaim, and the rest of my morning routine goes awry as I struggle to figure out what could have gone wrong.

So, I took up the role of monitoring and maintaining the airflow jobs prepared by the engineering team. Over time, I have encountered too many scenarios like the one described above that challenged my perception of handling failures.

In this article, I will communicate two things:

  • A mindset change.
  • A framework for handling failures.

Mindset change

1. Things can go wrong

I used to feel very disappointed when a job I created failed. I thought it was an indictment against my competence. But one of the first things I observed in the more senior members of my team is they were always more relaxed when errors popped up.

Suffice it to say, I understood that Edward Murphy was right. Developing a mindset that things can go wrong helped me achieve two things:

  • I began to write more failure proof scripts(if you work with redshift you’d understand that this,… well the least said the better)
  • I was less critical of myself when my scripts failed. I took it as an opportunity to learn more about the system and write better code.
That, things can go wrong, may seem like a pessimistic stance but you are more likely to improve faster by learning from your failures than you would from your successes.

2. No blame games!

Nobody likes to have their daily routine disrupted because some pipelines decided to fail. You are likely to be grumpy and look for someone or something to chew up; fair enough. But it does not do much good.

In the event of a failure, what you do not want to do is look for someone to blame. Instead, focus on; finding out what the incident is, its impact and the resolution.

People naturally become defensive and are likely to absolve themselves of any fault when things go wrong. Playing the blame game increases tension within the team and stops anyone from arriving at the root cause early enough.

Having mindset changes is one of the many internal work you should anticipate doing throughout your career. It provides a faster route to develop.

A framework for handling failures.

One of the many lessons I learned from reading Matthew Syed’s book, Blackbox Thinking was that: The way to improve the efficiency of any system is to learn from the times when the system failed. And that this usually requires that individuals and teams be objective enough to prevent emotions and ego from interfering.

Over time I observed a practice among my engineering team, and I came up with a routine to help me handle the errors much more quickly. The following describes this further:

1. Do a preliminary analysis and gauge the impact of the error.

i. What job failed?

The alert email and the generated logs will usually contain that information. (this assumes the logs are being written to the Airflow UI and that each task in the airflow job has the email_on_failure option set to True)

ii. Are there dependent jobs?

Here you want to quickly find out if other jobs depend on the output generated by the failed job. They could be a tableau report or a python script that handles some extra complex transformations. Finding out the dependent jobs helps you gauge which other systems will be affected.

2. Communicate to stakeholders.

This step is vital as you want to be the first to highlight the problem before the business teams ring the alarm bells. Armed with the information gathered from the previous step, you can quickly draft a short message/email informing them of the error and the systems that are to be affected.

Communicate to your engineering team as well.

3. Deep dive into the incident and work out the fix.

In this step, you identify the root cause and work out a fix. The time spent here depends on the error and perhaps technical skills but be sure to collaborate with a teammate as soon as you are stuck. Don’t forget that the goal is to arrive at the root cause and work out a fix as soon as possible.

When the fix has been tested and applied, communicate back to the engineering team and the business stakeholders.

4. Document, document, document!

I must admit this is the hardest and most mundane step. After resolving the error and applying the fix, the last thing you want to do is prepare a write-up.

But this is a vital component because errors reveal faults. They are like feedback mechanisms that show you where the problem was. By documenting, you expose that new knowledge for posterity. I think that’s why StackOverflow will forever remain a gold mine.

Aim for brevity. The documentation should contain:

  • What the error was, add screenshots where available.
  • What was the root cause?
  • The fix that was applied.
  • Any recommendation to prevent future occurrence.

In concluding, accepting that things can sometimes go wrong and not looking for someone to blame when they do, can be a game-changer.

So when the error alerts pop up, you can run through this process:

  1. Do a preliminary analysis and gauge the impact of the error.
  2. Communicate to stakeholders.
  3. Deep dive into the incident and work out the fix.
  4. Document, document, document!

I admit this may seem like a lot of work. But, you are likely to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying tech architecture. And perhaps more importantly, this can also reveal to me how deeply connected your work is with the rest of the business.

And as if by some miracle, we now receive fewer error alerts.

I found this article by Kiana Alessandra Villaera on how to mitigate against fixing bugs for Data engineers. Do check it out.

I hope you enjoyed this.

Cheers!!

entry.title: 6 months a data engineer…
entry.content:
So I landed a data engineering role and I was buzzing to get started. Finally, I was going to test my scripting skills in a business environment, I thought to myself.

My focus was simple too; write better and more efficient scripts and write them faster.

After 6 months my perspectives have changed quite a bit, although I’m well on my way to reaching my initial goal, I’ve had to unlearn and pick up some new behaviour.

The following is my attempt to articulate some of the lessons learned, some quite the hard way. So here goes, in no particular order:

Understand the business context.

I had read countless blogs posts on data engineering that stressed its importance but it never really quite dawned till I found myself on the job.

I quickly found that the data engineering role meant, you’re going to be at the receiving end of the majority of the data that is used by the company, data really really familiar to them.

I know the temptation is to jump right into the coding but do spend some time to get familiar with the operations of the various departments.

Learn the terminologies, understand what the abbreviations represent, identify the metrics and KPIs that will be thrown around you.

The entire codebase can be initially daunting!

I was a little over-ambitious when I began, I set off to try to understand the entire code-base no matter the cost.

A noble cause yes but reality slowly dawned on me that business wasn’t going to slow down for me to catch up. And I ended up over-exerting time and energy trying to satisfy my curiosity which was still painfully short.

I learned a key lesson though, focus on the business use case rather than the fine details of the code. Every project folder, script or query addresses a specific use case and wading through the code base with that as a guide can help you quickly make sense of the code little by little. Then over time as you complete more tasks, you build a better intuition of the code.

So take it slow, you’re not expected to have the entire codebase in your head. Just focus on knowing enough so you know where to look.

Ask. Ask. Ask!

It doesn’t mean you’re dumb!

This hurt me one time when I completed a ticket late because I felt it was my responsibility to figure out any confusion by myself.

After failing on this several times I learned the approach of typing a quick summary after each project meeting and sharing it with the stakeholder.

Aim to seek clarity before undertaking any assigned task. Engage the task issuer as soon as soon can be, jump on a quick call if you have to. It really shows you’re paying attention and you will deliver on tasks much much faster.

So brace yourself to be naive and painfully clueless at times. Don’t try to understand everything on your own, ask ask and ask!

You will make mistakes, Just own it!

When I started, I put an unhealthy amount of pressure on myself to prove my worth. So much so that anytime I made a mistake or do something terribly wrong, I began to doubt my competence.

Things happen yes just don’t beat yourself over it!

Expect to make mistakes every once in a while but focus on owning them. I found that this was a much faster approach to making fewer mistakes overall.

Owning your mistake means alerting your team as soon as possible and providing solutions to fix it, so it can be corrected.

Saying: “it is my fault” is not that hard and you quickly become a more trustworthy person in your team.

Say something!

I struggled with this initially, I just wanted to work in my small corner and produce the needed output, but I quickly found that my outputs as a data engineer depended on the inputs of several others and so it wasn’t that prudent.

Giving periodic updates to your stakeholders is one of the surest proofs that you’re working.

Communicate blockers too, you do not only yourself but your team and sometimes the larger business a disservice if you fail to communicate blockers in a timely manner.

This was hard for me because I saw it as defeat if I communicated my blockers but yeah things caught up to me fast. So I developed a system for asking for help:

  • For code blockers, I give myself up to 3 hours then I ask for help.
  • For issues with clarity of task requirements, I raise the flag immediately.

Well, I’m getting better at this, but yeah, communicate, communicate communicate.

Learn more about yourself

June 2022 will mark my 3rd active working year since I graduated. So I still think it’s the early days in my career. There’s a great deal more I can know, and I feel I’m only getting started.

During my culture fit interview session, I stumbled on a question on work-life balance. I hadn’t considered this before. So I didn’t really know what an ideal working environment looked like. So this lesson was perhaps the most important lesson I had to learn: Know thyself!!

Capture the feedback that will be communicated to you, take them in your stride and keep on moving.

Learn about yourself, be intentional about identifying what works for you; Maybe you’d find that your day gets messed up if you respond to emails early morning, Or that you thrive with minimal supervision than micromanaging, Or that you tend to do great work when there are no distractions around.

Whatever it is, learn about yourself and use that to plan your working day.

Over time you’re going to build a great intuition, which would help inform your next career step.

Finally, I really think it is a long road to mastery, and it takes time to build competency. So slow down, browse through some programming memes and laugh at yourself every once in a while.

PS: If you want a quick intro to Data Engineering do check this post by a good colleague.

Hope you enjoyed this.
Cheers!!
